questions.stem: The Latin root 'port' means 'to carry'. What exactly does the word 'portable' mean?

options.option_text: A very large, permanently fixed, unmovable physical building.
Able to be easily carried or moved from one place to another.
A completely invisible gaseous substance. (alternative interpretation)
An object that has been completely destroyed. (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: 'Portable' combines 'port' (carry) and '-able' (capable of). It describes something that is designed to be easily carried.

questions.stem: Combining the prefix 'im-' (into) and the root 'port' (carry), what does 'import' exactly mean in trade?

options.option_text: To destroy all locally produced domestic goods. (alternative interpretation)
To give away free products to poor local farmers.
To bring goods or services into a country from abroad for sale.
To stop all international trading immediately. (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: To 'import' means to bring (goods or services) into a country from abroad for sale. It literally means 'carry into'.

questions.stem: Combining the prefix 'ex-' (out) and the root 'port', what does 'export' exactly mean?

options.option_text: To buy products exclusively from foreign companies.
To refuse to sell local items completely. (alternative interpretation)
To permanently close a large trading harbor.
To send goods or services to another country for sale.

questions.explanation: To 'export' means to send (goods or services) to another country for sale. It literally means 'carry out'.

questions.stem: The prefix 'trans-' means 'across'. What exactly does 'transport' fundamentally mean?

options.option_text: To take or carry people or goods from one place to another.
To quickly change a person's physical appearance completely.
To translate a foreign language into a local dialect.
To suddenly disappear without any prior warning.

questions.explanation: To 'transport' means to take or carry (people or goods) from one place to another. It translates literally to 'carry across'.

questions.stem: What exactly is a 'portfolio' in the context of the root word 'port'?

options.option_text: A massive ocean vessel used exclusively for military transport. (alternative interpretation)
A tiny digital storage device holding musical tracks. (alternative interpretation)
A large, thin, flat case used for carrying loose sheets of paper, drawings, or maps.
A specialized musical instrument that is very difficult to play. (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: A 'portfolio' (from 'portare' to carry + 'foglio' leaf/sheet) is a flat case for carrying loose sheets of paper, or metaphorically a range of investments or pieces of work.

questions.stem: The prefix 'de-' means 'away'. In law, what exactly does it mean to 'deport' someone?

options.option_text: To warmly welcome a new political refugee legally.
To officially expel a foreigner from a country.
To formally grant immediate national citizenship to a foreigner.
To quietly hire a foreign worker for a highly skilled job.

questions.explanation: To 'deport' means to officially expel a foreigner from a country. It translates directly to 'carry away'.

questions.stem: The prefix 'com-' means 'with'. What exactly does the formal word 'comport' mean?

options.option_text: To legally quickly cancel a previously signed legal contract.
To physically comfort a crying or deeply upset child.
To forcefully forcefully break down a heavily locked thick door.
To conduct oneself or behave in a particular manner.

questions.explanation: To 'comport' oneself means to conduct oneself or behave in a particular manner. It literally means 'to carry oneself with'.

questions.stem: The word 'reportage' derives from 're-' (back) + 'port' (carry). In journalism, 'reportage' most precisely refers to which of the following?

options.option_text: an editorial opinion piece that argues a political standpoint
a structured interview conducted with a prominent public figure
the factual, on-the-spot carrying back of events as news
a fictional narrative that deliberately mimics news writing style

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'reportage' etymologically means carrying news back (re- = back, port = carry) and refers to factual, first-hand journalistic coverage of events. Option A describes an editorial column, which involves opinion rather than carrying back facts. Option B describes an interview format; Option D describes 'new journalism' fiction — neither fits the etymological core of 'carrying back' direct, factual events.

questions.stem: Etymologically, 'support' (sub- = under + port = carry) most precisely conveys which of the following meanings?

options.option_text: to praise or commend someone for exceptional achievements
to carry the weight of something firmly from underneath
to carry an argument forward using documented evidence
to move something carefully from one location to another

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'sub-' means under/below and 'port' means carry, so 'support' literally means to carry from beneath — to bear up, sustain, or hold up. Option C is a tempting distractor since we do 'support an argument', but that usage is metaphorical; the root meaning is physical bearing from below. Option D confuses 'support' with the act of transport; Option A confuses it with commendation.

questions.stem: Etiquette academies historically taught 'deportment' as a core finishing skill. Given that 'port' means 'to carry', which description best defines 'deportment'?

options.option_text: the formal legal procedure for expelling a foreign national
the freight and shipping charges applied to export consignments
an authoritative written report filed by a senior government officer
one's overall bearing, posture, and manner of social conduct

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'deportment' means the way one carries oneself — posture, bearing, and social conduct (how one 'carries' their body and manners). Option A is the classic trap: candidates confuse 'deportment' with 'deportation' (expelling someone from a country), but deportment concerns personal bearing, not legal removal. Options B and C involve unrelated meanings grafted onto the '-port' sound.

questions.stem: In adventure sports and historical inland trade, 'portage' (from Latin 'portare' = to carry) refers to which specific activity?

options.option_text: carrying a canoe or cargo overland between two waterways
steering a boat through dangerous shallow rapids using poles
fastening cargo securely with ropes before a long sea voyage
loading and unloading trade goods at a commercial harbour

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'portage' means carrying boats, canoes, or cargo overland past an obstacle — a waterfall, rapids, or a land stretch between two rivers. This was crucial on exploration and trade routes. Option B describes 'shooting rapids' or 'poling'. Option D confuses portage with harbour activity — a port is a place; portage is the act of carrying between ports or waterways. Option C describes cargo lashing.

questions.stem: The verb 'purport' (Latin: pro- = forward + portare = carry) is correctly defined by which of the following?

options.option_text: to carry an urgent official despatch across national boundaries
to openly protest a decision made by an authoritative body
to arrange transport of goods using multiple freight carriers
to claim or appear to be something, often without solid proof

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'purport' means to claim or profess to be something — to carry forward an apparent or intended meaning (e.g., 'The document purports to be signed by the Minister'). Options A and C are traps that exploit the 'carry' root by linking it to physical transport of dispatches or freight. Option B confuses 'purport' with 'protest' due to a similar formal register and sound pattern.

questions.stem: A job applicant is described as 'importunate' in demanding a promotion. Which nuance best distinguishes 'importunate' from merely 'persistent'?

options.option_text: importunate describes persistence that is logical and firmly evidence-based
importunate implies persistence that is troublesome and disregards others' convenience
importunate refers to persistence that is restrained and avoids confrontation
importunate denotes persistence confined specifically to commercial negotiations

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'importunate' (from Latin 'importunus' = not at the harbour, i.e., untimely, inconvenient) means annoyingly persistent — pressing demands at the wrong time, disregarding others' comfort. Unlike mere persistence, which can be admirable, importunate behaviour is intrusive and harassing. Option A describes 'tenacious'; Option C describes 'discreet persistence'; Option D wrongly limits the word to trade or commercial contexts.

questions.stem: The archaic English verb 'disport' (dis- = away + port = carry oneself) meant to carry oneself away from work for recreation. Which modern English word descended directly from 'disport' by dropping its prefix?

options.option_text: resort — carrying oneself repeatedly back to a favoured place
export — carrying goods away from the country of origin
sport — carrying oneself away from daily toil into recreation
report — carrying information back to the original source

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'sport' is directly derived from Middle English 'disport' by dropping the prefix 'dis-'. 'Disport' meant to divert or amuse oneself (carry oneself away from work), and the shortened form 'sport' retained this sense of recreation and play — which is why we still speak of sport as leisure. Option A ('resort') comes from French 'ressortir' (to go out again) — a different root entirely. Options B and D ('export', 'report') are common PORT-root words but are not derived from 'disport'.
